utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution is cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Grujicic. Can you hear us quite clearly this morning?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. I can hear you clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Today I'm just going to ask you if you could possibly listen very carefully to the questions that I ask you and just answer that question, and don't give a large explanation unless I ask you for an explanation. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do understand. I tried to keep that in mind yesterday and to consider my answers carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be aware, I want as concise an answer as possible. If you can answer it yes or no, please do so, because Mr. Lukic will ask you anything afterwards that needs to be clarified, and he's very aware of what I'm asking. So please bear that in mind. Now, yesterday, Mr. Grujicic, in giving your evidence, you gave evidence or you told us that you were a humanist or a humanitarian. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As a humanist, you would have been appalled by the war that was going on in the former Yugoslavia in the early 1990s, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was appalled.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were also appalled as a humanist by the practice of ethnic cleansing, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I wasn't working on any kind of ethnic cleansing, nor did I see any of the civilian commissions do any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I just ask you to concentrate, please, on the question I asked you. I asked you: As a humanist, a person concerned for humanitarian things, you would have been appalled by any ethnic cleansing that occurred, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I focused well on your question, and I told you that I had no occasion to see any ethnic cleansing. But rather, the passage of civilian population through corridors in order to bring families back together, that's what I was appalled by.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was asking you whether you would have been appalled by ethnic cleansing. Please concentrate and confine yourself to the question, please. Now, the Special Rapporteur of the United Nations went to Bosnia-Herzegovina several times in 1991, 1992, and 1993. The Special Rapporteur reported back to the United Nations on ethnic cleansing in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991, 1992, and 1993. Do you understand that? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Will you just excuse me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only thing I don't understand is why you're referring to 1991 and Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was no war there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This is what the Special Rapporteur found in his report -- third report of the 17th of November, 1992, Mr. Grujicic. Please just listen to this, and I'll read it to you. I'm reading paragraph 8: "Ethnic cleansing is the direct cause of the vast majority of human rights violations which have occurred in Bosnia and Herzegovina since the present human rights emergency began in March and April 1992." Paragraph 9: "The term 'ethnic cleansing' refers to the elimination by the ethnic group exercising control over a given territory of members of other ethnic groups, a wide variety of methods are used to accomplish this end, including threats, harassment, and intimidation." I won't read the rest of that paragraph. Paragraph 10: "Ethnic cleansing is often accompanied by confiscation of the property of those forced to leave, including homes, farms, and agricultural equipment. In some areas, homes and farm buildings have been razed in order to preclude any possibility of return. Departure often involves long and arduous journeys, during which the displaced population is systematically robbed of savings, jewellery, and other personal effects, exposed to beatings and rape, deprived of food and shelter, in many instances, the fleeing population has been obliged to cross through areas of armed conflict." That, Mr. Grujicic, is what the Special Rapporteur reported back to the United Nations in 1992 on what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Are you telling the Trial Chamber that as a member of the 1st Krajina Corps's commission for exchanges, that you were unaware of what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no time to ponder those issues, if they were indeed as you say they were. I fought for human lives. I or any other members of any of the commissions were not involved in any kind of ethnic cleansing. There was civil war. Certainly there was a lot of fear, a lot of misfortune. But as for your question, I think it needs to be answered by someone else, if that's the way you choose to phrase it. I only worked on the exchanges of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying even 10 years after the event you won't agree that ethnic cleansing occurred in Bosnia-Herzegovina by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By no means. The civil war was caused by fear, on all sides. You can't emphasise one aspect or one side. If there was indeed any such thing. But on my side, or rather, where I worked, there was no ethnic cleansing. We didn't do that part of the job. I think the International Red Cross was best placed to monitor that. They were always with us attending the exchanges of prisoners of war and all the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Special Rapporteur disagreed with you, Mr. Grujicic. In paragraph 9 of the same report, that is, made on the ground in November 1992, they reported this: "In Bosnia and Herzegovina, ethnic cleansing is practiced systematically by Serbs in order to expel Muslims, Croats, and smaller ethnic groups from areas under their control. In some areas, including the area west of Banja Luka, the objective of ethnic cleansing has been largely accomplished. A large percentage of the Muslim and Croat population has already left or is confined to a camp or another -- of one kind or another. The vast majority of the remaining Muslim and Croat population is anxious to leave as soon as it is materially possible to do so." That's what the Special Rapporteur went on to say in his report. Are you still disagreeing that ethnic cleansing was perpetrated by Serb forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree. The reason I disagree is that the gentleman probably only visited one of the sides, and it just seemed to him like that. I must repeat this: This was civil war caused by fear, caused by anxiety felt by all the people and by all the different ethnic groups. I'm not introducing any separation between Croats, Serbs, and Muslims there. And certainly there was a certain amount of fear because the war had started. Ethnic cleansing, what does that mean? That means that we should gather all non-Serb or non-Croat or non-Muslim population of a given town and move it to a different area. There was no such thing happening. At least not in the areas of the Banja Luka sector. There were only agreements between civilian commissions. The gentlemen from Zenica, from Travnik, from Tuzla, and from the whole area, from Orasje, from Croatia, and so on and so forth, and what they would agree which was in principle to bring families back together, what I talked about yesterday, I certainly don't consider that to be an example of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So your evidence is, is it, there was no ethnic cleansing in Bosnia-Herzegovina by Serb forces during the civil war? Is that your evidence? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, all the points of transit where I worked, or where we worked, I did not notice any such thing happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. My question was: Is your evidence that there was no ethnic cleansing by Serb forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the answer by the witness was clear. He's a witness of fact. And in answer to your question, he clearly said that in view of his activity, he saw no such thing happening. Now they're asking the witness to speculate whether any such thing was happening in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The witness, however, on page 6 of the transcript, clearly said that he saw no such thing happening and that he was not involved in any such thing. This is not an expert witness; this is a factual witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll move to another area, Your Honour. I won't press that question at the moment in that form.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, can you please just tell us, to refresh us from yesterday, just the areas in which you worked. Just list them, please, going from one side of Bosnia to the other. No explanation; just the areas, please.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the areas of the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The areas -- okay. I'll refine that question. The areas under Serb control in Bosnia-Herzegovina where you worked in 1992 and 1993. Please just list the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosanska Gradiska, Bosanska Dubica, Prijedor, Banja Luka, Donji Vakuf, Donje Knezevo, Kotor Vares, Teslic, Doboj, then the whole of Ozren, Modrica, Samac, Derventa, Bosanski Brod, and Srbac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you're telling the Trial Chamber, are you, that in all of those areas, Bosanska Gradiska, Dubica, Prijedor, Banja Luka, Donji Vakuf, Novo -- whatever it is, I'm sorry -- Kotor Vares, Teslic, Doboj, Ozren, Modrica, Samac, Derventa, Bosanski Brod, and Srbac in 1992 and 1993 --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Kotor Vares.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In all the time you worked there in 1992 and 1993 on the commission for exchanges, you saw absolutely no evidence that Muslims and Croats were being forced to move from their homes by Serb forces? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that I was a humanist by conviction, a humanitarian person, I meant I wasn't carrying any weapons. I was not on the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you please answer my question. My question is whether you --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I saw no such thing happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you're telling the Trial Chamber, are you, that you heard nothing in that time of the forcible removal of Muslims and Croats from their homes or areas in 1992 and 1993 while you were working across those ranges of municipalities? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw no such thing. I didn't even know which villages were Serb dominated and which villages were Croat or Muslim dominated, or towns, for that matter. There were burnt villages on all sides, but there was no way for me to distinguish, and I simply had no time to consider these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please concentrate on the question. The question wasn't what you saw; the question was what you heard. You're telling the Trial Chamber you heard of no incidents of Muslims and Croats being forced to leave their homes and territories by Serb forces in 1992 and 1993 while you were working across those broad ranges of municipalities; is that your evidence? You heard nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My dear gentleman, I heard nothing. I was only meeting people who were seeking our assistance, and I didn't go about those villages investigating. We would go directly to the approved points of transit for the exchanges. So the answer is: I heard nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In all the time you were working on General Talic's staff as the chairman of his Exchange Commission, you heard nothing about ethnic cleansing by Serb forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that still your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I stand by that. That is my testimony. When you said that I worked on the staff, that's not true. I didn't work on the staff. We merely had our headquarters in the same building, but I was myself not a high official of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As a humanist, of course, you would have been appalled by ethnic cleansing if you had known it was going on, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have been appalled, and if I had been in a position to help anyone, I would have helped, and that's precisely what I was doing for the whole duration of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As a humanist, you would have been appalled if Serb forces had been expelling people from their homes and forcing them into detention centres, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You would have been appalled if the Serb leadership was pursuing a policy of ethnic separation by force, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly. Because that didn't happen. I told you: There was a civil war. I didn't tell you that one people caused ill to another people. It was civil war. This goes for both sides. But I don't want to get mixed up in that, because I was not into politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As a humanist, you would have been appalled -- you told us yesterday you're a humanist. You would have been appalled if non-Serbs were locked up in detention centres by Serb forces and forced to endure inhumane conditions. You would have been appalled by that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already answered that yesterday by objecting, both to Mr. Todorovic and to Mr. General, because Croats had been beaten who were on their way to an exchange. As proof of that, can you please look at this title. This is my book, a book I wrote, and the title translates as: "The graves of war cause me pain." And I wasn't referring to Serb graves only; I was referring to Croat graves and Muslim graves too. I can send you a copy of this book so you can survey all the work that we humanists did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you humanists -- I withdraw that. In this book you've just shown us, is there any reference there to Serb ethnic cleansing between 1992 and 1993 in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or is that missing from your book?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no such thing, because no such thing is part of this book. The people included in this book are the people who needed our help, the detained, those who had gone missing, and those who had been killed. When you speak about ethnic cleansing, that's simply not part of this book. If any such thing happened indeed, there will be someone else, I'm sure, to write a book about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You would agree that if someone had been locked up by the Serb forces only because they were non-Serb, put into a detention centre and left there until they were exchanged, that would fall within the definition of ethnic cleansing, wouldn't it, Mr. Grujicic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think so. There were judicial organs. Those judicial organs did their job, their tasks. They processed the detainees who were in our area. After processing, we could begin to carry out the exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So your evidence to the Trial Chamber is, is it, that everyone who was in Serb detention was there according to some sort of judicial order or judicial process, during 1992 and 1993? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not my evidence. I do not know whether all the people were processed or not. I only know about those who were requested to be exchanged. We could only exchange them once they had been processed. But I never went to prisons. I never visited prisons so that I could know any of those people. That was a different team working on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As a humanist, you, of course, would agree with the rights of all people under a democratic constitution to vote to elect their leaders, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And as a humanist --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As a humanist, of course, you would be appalled if one ethnic group had taken over the government of various municipalities in Bosnia to the exclusion of others in government, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. I don't know about the structure of government in the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not from the Banja Luka area. I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm asking you as a humanist, the humanist principles you told us about yesterday, Mr. Grujicic, as a humanist and, you've just said, someone who believes in democracy, you would be appalled if one ethnic group took over the reign -- forcibly took over power from the elected government, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Objection. Just a minute, Mr. Grujicic. This whole line of questioning by the Prosecutor's questions, I chose not to object, but I think I could have rightly done so right from the beginning. Personally, I think the emphasis that the Prosecution seems to be putting on the term "humanist" cannot provide ground for asking the witness these background questions, and this whole line of questioning refers to the witness's views and attitudes. When he spoke as a humanist yesterday, he spoke about the facts I had asked him about. This line of questioning, I understand if you ask this line of questioning to Professor Nikolic, an expert witness, but I think if you pose these questions to a witness who already told us that he had no information on certain facts, calls, I think, for mere speculation. This is a game of hide and seek which the witness is expected to take part in. I think if we want him to tell us about facts, then this term "humanist" can certainly give no extra room for the Prosecution to ask such questions, except as related to what the witness told us about in the first part of his examination-in-chief, namely, the exchanges. But I think this whole line of questioning is driving at something altogether different, not the exchanges themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I briefly respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber is of the view that the Prosecution can pursue that line of questioning, because the questions go to the credibility of the witness. The only caution [Realtime transcript read in error "question"] is that avoid repetition.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Look, I was asking you, as a humanist, about your attitude to the forcible takeover of democratically elected institutions by Serb forces, that is, the forces of one ethnicity forcibly taking over the democratic institutions of the entire municipality or country. I'm asking you whether, as a humanist, that would have appalled you.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to answer you in a different way. In Banja Luka, the vice-president of the municipality was a representative of the HDZ. I got to know him because I cooperated with him, in connection with exchanges of war prisoners. Therefore, there was no cleansing that I can see, when the representative of the HDZ was the vice-president of the municipality. I can't speak about other areas. Would I have been horrified? Don't ask me that. Ask me about the entire territory, the territory of Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Republika Srpska. Of course I'm horrified. Why did this happen? But leave me alone, because I, as a humanist, only fought to save human lives. I did not want to be involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So as a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, yes. Before you continue, I just wanted to correct the transcript. Line 21, page 12. I didn't say the only question. I said, "The only caution is avoid repetition." And I'd like to inform Mr. Grujicic that he should only answer questions as they are put to him and not explain. If he disagrees, he should say so. So please, Mr. Grujicic, listen to the question and just answer the question as it is put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: On my last question, are you saying that as a humanist you don't have a position or a moral position on forcible ethnic takeover by Serbs of democratically elected institutions?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no position on this. I did not deal with that. I have proved that in Banja Luka there was a Croat who was the vice-president of the municipality, and he was the president of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't ask you about Banja Luka. But listen: As a humanist, surely you would have been appalled by the massacre of thousands of Muslim men and boys at Srebrenica by the Drina Corps, which was part of your own army in 1995. You would have been appalled by that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any death horrifies me. Until it is proved who the perpetrator is, I cannot say that it was done by one particular side. I know what happened in our area. Srebrenica is far away from our area. And what happened later, and what the media are reporting today, I'm not interested in that. I write books about what I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you are going outside the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So the question about Srebrenica 1995 and the answer will be struck off the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was only putting it as to his credibility and his understanding as to ethnic cleansing, which is part of the indictment, Your Honour, and his belief and understanding, only as to credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but you stick to the issues that happened during the period covered by the indictment; otherwise we'll be getting outside the indictment, and that is not what we're supposed to be doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There's enough material, end of 1991, 1992, 1993, covered by the indictment, which you can use to test his credibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, you, of course, as a humanist, would have been appalled if the prisoners -- or appalled by the use of prisoners detained in Serb detention facilities for forced labour and trench-digging on the front line. That would have appalled you as a humanist, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would have appalled me. But I don't agree with you when you accuse one side exclusively. I am horrified when any prisoner is used in an illegal way to do things he should not have to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A little bit earlier when I questioned you about -- or put to you what the Special Rapporteur had reported on, you responded that that was only concentrating on one side, the ethnic cleansing there, and you didn't agree with it. If I told you that the Special Rapporteur also reported on the ethnic cleansing of Serbs by the Croats and breaches of international humanitarian law by the Bosnian Federation government, would that change your view as to the objectivity of the United Nations Special Rapporteur's report, where he found there was ethnic cleansing being perpetrated by Serbs in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will again answer as I answered before. Within the framework of my job, I was not able to observe ethnic cleansing on this basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You are aware, are you not, that Mrs. Biljana Plavsic was sentenced last week by the Trial Chamber -- by a Trial Chamber in The Hague for persecuting non-Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina? You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many things I don't know. But what have I got to do with a high-ranking official whom I have never seen or had the opportunity to contact?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My question was: Were you aware -- are you aware that she was sentenced last week for persecution, after pleading guilty to it? That's all. Are you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I have not seen the indictment, nor do I know about the sentence, but I have heard about the conviction.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said earlier that ethnic cleansing, as far as you were concerned, didn't occur. If I tell you that Mrs. Plavsic has pleaded guilty to it and signed a document in which she agreed that she and the Serb -- Bosnian Serb leadership pursued the objective of ethnic separation by force, would that change your view as to whether ethnic cleansing occurred in Bosnia in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No, that would not change my opinion. Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, if she stated something, is to be held responsible for it. But I am stating what I have said here. I was not able to observe any ethnic cleansing in the area and during the time that I was working on these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. Mrs. Plavsic said - and I'll read to you what she said, paragraph 11 of her plea agreement, or the factual basis underlying her plea of guilty. Listen carefully, please: "In October 1991 and the months following, the SDS intensified efforts to ensure that the objective of ethnic separation by force would be achieved, in the event that a negotiated solution did not occur. These steps included arming large segments of the Bosnian Serb population, in collaboration with others, the JNA, the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Serbia, the Serbian paramilitaries, establishing Serbian military and police formations, and coordinating with the JNA and paramilitary units from inside and outside Bosnia-Herzegovina." Paragraph 13: "Numerous individuals participated in devising and executing the objective of ethnic separation by force, including Slobodan Milosevic, Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, and Ratko Mladic." In paragraph 19: "The Bosnian Serb military, police and civilian forces and authorities, under the direction and control of the SDS, and authorities of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including the collective presidency and the expanded collective presidency, collaborated with the JNA, the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Serbia, and paramilitary units from within and outside Bosnia-Herzegovina to implement this objective of ethnic separation by force. The Bosnian Serb military police and civilian forces, collaborating with the JNA, the MUP of Serbia and paramilitary units committed persecutions upon the non-Serb population through a persecutory campaign that included the events and locations contained in the indictment." Now, that, Mr. Grujicic, is what Mrs. Plavsic, the president of Bosnia, has admitted to doing -- I'm sorry, president of the Republika Srpska - has admitted to doing and has been sentenced to 11 years imprisonment for doing, taking part in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fairness to the witness, my learned friend should specify when Mrs. Plavsic was president of Republika Srpska. Is that in the period of 1992, 1993, which is covered by our indictment, or he's speaking about the -- her indictment? So it might be confused for this witness. And also if he can specify whether the municipality of Samac is included in her indictment, and then to establish certain foundation why this witness should be relevant for this line of questioning. So it's just a suggestion. I mean, it's not objection in strict form. I mean, it would be fair for this witness and it would be fair for the defendants and for this process to establish all these elements. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. Perhaps there is need to clarify, so that the witness understands. Maybe he does not know. I know that the proceedings were over and it's an official record of the Tribunal, but maybe the witness may not have known the period that she was president of the Republic of Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just one moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If it assists you, Mr. Grujicic, Mrs. Plavsic was the acting president of the Republika Srpska between the 28th of February, 1992, and the 12th of May, 1992, and from the 12th of May that year, she was a member of the three-member presidency. And from June 1992 until 17th of December, 1992, she was a member of the expanded presidency of the Bosnian Serb Republic. Just to put it all in context. What I just read to you was a document Mrs. Plavsic signed in admitting her complicity in a campaign to persecute non-Serbs throughout large areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina. She has pleaded guilty to ethnic cleansing. She said it happened, and she was one of the people orchestrating it. Does that change your view as to whether or not -- or sorry, will you now change your evidence as to whether or not ethnic cleansing occurred in Bosnia and Herzegovina - I'll finish the question - in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. Grujicic. Please wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor responded to only the first half of my colleague Mr. Pantelic's objection, but not the other part. I'm not asking that the Prosecutor now read out the entire territory covered by the indictment against Mrs. Plavsic, but simply to confirm that among the 35 municipalities, whether the municipality of Samac is mentioned at all in the indictment or not, because the witness should know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That, with respect to my learned friend, has nothing to do with the proposition I'm putting to the witness, which relates to ethnic cleansing in Bosnia-Herzegovina and goes to his credit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Mr. Lukic. There is no need for the Prosecutor to point out whether or not Bosanski Samac was covered. Mr. Re, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember the question, Mr. Grujicic? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer you in this way. You read to me probably a party platform. Yesterday I told Mr. Lukic that I did not belong to any party, nor was I interested in the political aspect. What Mrs. Plavsic, or somebody else, did, they will be held accountable and punished for. But I abide by my statement that my job was not to conduct ethnic cleansing, and we did not do so. You have to ask other people about everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, so you're saying that Mrs. Plavsic's admission to orchestrating ethnic cleansing by the Serbs throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina in the period we're concerned with here, and her being sentenced to 11 years' gaol for doing so, and her setting out how she did it with the Serb leaders and the JNA and the army of which you were a member, does not in any way change your view as to whether or not ethnic cleansing occurred? The fact that she has admitted to orchestrating it doesn't alter in any way your view that it did occur; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I disagree with your thesis, and I have nothing to say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yesterday you gave some evidence, Mr. Grujicic -- or I asked you some questions about the exchanges, the specific -- exchanges you were involved in and the principle of a one-for-one exchange. Do you remember that evidence? Just a yes or no. I don't want an explanation, please.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And I just want to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown or put on the ELMO D162/3 ter, D162/3 ter. While that's being sought, I'll show the witness another document. I'm going to show the witness PDB 91/3, which doesn't have an exhibit number yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, we're putting a document on the screen. Can you see the document?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not well. Not well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It appears that we've given you the wrong document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could I have that document back, please? There seems to be nine names on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It mentions Bijeljina. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, can you sort out the document you need to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Your Honour. Yes. I had them all here. One moment, please. I'll move on to something else. We've just got to sort out some documents here, Mr. Grujicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, I just want to ask you some things about detention and the exchanges. Now, the Serbs took over the town of Prijedor on the 30th of April, 1992. It was the SDS and the JNA took control of that town on the 30th of April, 1992. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... The events in Prijedor with Samac. I mean let's first maybe hear the foundation of this line of questioning from our learned friends and then we could see what's going on. Because otherwise, if now we are opening Prijedor -- I don't simply understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Probably the witness neither understands too. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If I could be allowed to continue my questioning, I'll get to the point very, very quickly. Several questions relate somewhere. That's all. It's cross-examination. It's what one does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You understand what I'm saying: The Serbs, took over, the SDS and the JNA took over Prijedor on the 30th of April, 1992. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was working in Banja Luka, and at that time the staff of the Krajina Corps was still in Stara Gradiska. During the war, I never visited Prijedor, but I did exchange their soldiers, who, for instance, were at positions near Gradacac, Pakrac, Lipik, and Novska, facing those towns. That was the extent of my connection with Prijedor. I know nothing about anything else, nor do I have any knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just telling you what happened: The Serbs took over. I just want you to accept the Serbs took over - for the purposes of the question I'm asking you - on the 30th of April, 1992. You will accept that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say that's what happened, it probably did, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just basing this on a judgement of the Tribunal in the Kvocka case. So I'm just telling you what happened, okay? The next thing that happened was the Serbs took control of a Muslim village of Hambarine on the 23rd of May, 1992, also found by the Trial Chamber. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can accept it, but no, I won't accept it, because I don't know where Hambarine is, nor have I ever been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As a result, and the Muslims counter-attacked in Prijedor on the 30th of May, 1992, and as a result of that, thousands of non-Serbs were rounded up and taken to three detention centres: Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje. Will you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would probably do well to ask someone else. What I know is that I arranged for the exchange of a brother -- I provided humanitarian assistance to the brother of the commander of the Bihac detachment. He had high blood sugar. He contracted hepatitis. I helped him to go to Zagreb to get proper treatment. That's the sort of thing I was involved in. It was down to others to think about what was happening to the different ethnic groups, the three ethnic groups. If it had been down to me, the whole thing would never have happened. So please don't ask me about areas that I personally have never visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the people who were taken to Keraterm, Omarska, and Trnopolje were separated into three categories, and the majority of people were sent to a camp called Manjaca. You're aware of Manjaca, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I was aware of Manjaca. At Manjaca, however, there was the commander who was in charge of that and who was taking care of that, and there were the judicial organs too, and that's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, the -- this is what the Trial Chamber -- you said you're aware of Manjaca. This is what the Trial Chamber in Kvocka found about people who were sent from Omarska and Keraterm to Manjaca. This is paragraph 19, talking about Omarska: "Everyone in the camp was interrogated at least once. The interrogations were typically accompanied by brutal physical and mental suffering. As a result of these interrogations, detainees were divided into three categories. The first contained those determined to pose the greatest threat to the Serb regime, defined as 'people who had directly organised and taken part in the armed rebellion.' The second consisted of 'people suspected of organising, abetting, financially and legally supplying arms' to the resistance group. And the third category was limited to those who were, in the words of Simo Drljaca of 'no security interest.' Those in the last category --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Slow down. Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "Those in the last category were originally slated to be transferred to Trnopolje or released. The others were to be sent to the 'prisoner of war' camp in Manjaca. Those in category 1 received the very worst treatment in Omarska, that is, those people -- the Trial Chamber in Kvocka found those people imprisoned in Omarska and subsequently went to Manjaca received the worst treatment, and the judgement details beatings, murders, sexual assault, and inhumane treatment." You understand, they went from Omarska to Manjaca? You understand what the Trial Chamber found: The prisoners in the worst condition from Omarska went to Manjaca. You understand what I'm saying to you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that prisoners were transferred to Manjaca, but the categories you spoke about, I have no idea about those. And all those we arranged for to be exchanged, the ones from Manjaca, I noticed nothing that you were talking about, namely, the beatings. I was dead against beatings. Therefore, I didn't notice any marks or traces of beatings when the exchanges were being carried out, but I never went to Manjaca myself, and I don't know what its rules were. There was a man there in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This is what the Special Rapporteur said about Manjaca, the prisoners you were exchanging, Mr. Grujicic. In his report of the 17th of November, 1992, the third report, at paragraph 33 he says: "Despite being denied access to the Manjaca prison camp, the Special Rapporteur has received ample information about conditions there. Most sources give the number of detainees --" may I finish the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You're in the middle of a quotation, so can you just complete the quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: " -- As being approximately 4.000 men who were housed in large open buildings formerly used as stables. Physical conditions were especially bad during the first several months after the detention facility was opened. Evidence of serious malnutrition, harsh discipline, strictly rationed water, poor sanitation, overcrowding, lack of proper medical care, and beating of prisoners has been received from a variety of credible sources. Physical conditions have improved somewhat since the camp began to be visited by international bodies in August. "The administrators of this facility, who are officials of the army of the Bosnian Serbs, maintain that the prisoners are prisoners of war. However, other observers consider that most of them probably never bore arms and were detained simply because of their age and Muslim ethnic origin made them potential combatants in the eyes of the Serbian authorities. The administrators of the Manjaca camp informed the Special Rapporteur that they looked forward to exchanging the prisoners at the earliest possible opportunity. This illustrates the role the detention of the Muslim and Croat civilian population plays in the ethnic cleansing -- plays in ethnic cleansing -" I'm sorry. "Those deprived of liberty for no reason accept their ethnic origin will be released only on the condition that they leave Serbian controlled territory. Few detainees are ever released and allowed to return to their homes in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, my question is, having read that quotation to you, is that you, Mr. Grujicic, on the 13th of January, 1993, you wrote to your humanist friend, Mr. Veljo Maslic, asking him to fax you a list of Croats and Muslims from Batkovic who had come from Manjaca. You said: "I'm interested in those who came from Manjaca to allow me to plan the next exchange." You asked Mr. Maslic to give you a list of the prisoners who had come from Manjaca in the conditions described by the Special Rapporteur, and according to the Special Rapporteur imprisoned only for the purposes of being taken for exchanges and ethnic cleansing, didn't you, Mr. Grujicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before the witness answers, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Grujicic, can you just hold on for a second. I have two objections to make, the first being, Your Honours, to this general line of questioning and its length. I complied with the Court order yesterday and I kept my line of questioning to the bare minimum. I tried to keep it as short as possible. We all know how strenuous videolink can be. The Prosecution focused on the women and the elderly people yesterday for 30 minutes. The witness told us very clearly that he knew nothing about the kind of treatment people were given at Manjaca, and yet the Prosecution is back to that line of questioning, with an extensive reading from the sentence. The second thing that my colleagues from the Prosecution did, they read from a document which they wanted to tender into evidence, where the list of prisoners to be sent from Manjaca to Batkovic is read out, but the document was shown yesterday, and this was wrongly attributed to Mr. Grujicic as asking for the list of prisoners from Batkovic. But the document clearly states: I am interested in people from Manjaca. I hope this can be explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Lukic can finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. I object to him saying this. He has the document. I object to him explaining to the witness what I'm doing. I don't mind him objecting. He has the document. He knows what the document is. I was going to put it to the witness, but I sat down to allow him to object. I object to him telling the witness what I'm intending to do with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. That's not what I wanted to say. I wanted to tell the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution misinterpreted the document. The Prosecution has given words which are not in the original documents, and that can easily mislead the witness. I, on the other hand, quoted the document as it was displayed on the ELMO. So it's the Prosecution that is trying to misinterpret the document here. May the document be again placed on the ELMO so that we can all see what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't understand that lengthy objection. I was about to put the document on the ELMO, but out the courtesy, I sat down to allow my friend to object, and he hasn't objected. So can I now put the document on the ELMO and show it to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The document should be put on the ELMO so that the witness can see it. Perhaps Mr. Lukic was objecting to the interpretation, which maybe he understood through your question. Let's have the document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Document PDB 84/3. Could the witness please be shown D177/3 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It has an exhibit number, doesn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Apparently it does. My information was incorrect, but apparently it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So what is the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, can you see that document which is D177/3?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you see it clearly --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I have another one in front of me that I can see more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The one I want to show you has -- no. Please, please. Can you see clearly the document dated 13th of January, 1993, to Velimir Maslic of Samac? Can you read it clearly? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am reading it, because I have it in front of me. The one I have in front of me is clearer for me to read than the one I can see on the screen, but it's the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please just read aloud the first paragraph, starting with "Veljo."

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Yesterday I forgot to tell you to fax me, immediately, the list of Croats and Muslims from Batkovic who have not been exchanged. I'm interested in those who came from Manjaca. I need that in order to plan further exchanges."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Stop there.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please be allowed to clarify this section?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Stop, please. What you've read out is exactly what it says; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. What I've read is exactly what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what you were saying there was that you were -- you were telling Mr. Maslic you were particularly interested in some prisoners who had come from Manjaca to Batkovic. That's what it says, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And I read you the extract from the Special Rapporteur's report about what he said about the reasons why people were detained in Manjaca, didn't I, in which he said --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have no problem with this, but this is already tendered into evidence, so if our learned colleague could give us a number for this exhibit. It's already on the exhibit list. Because there were quite a number of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He has already given the exhibit number. Yes, you can proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You're there expressing an interest in obtaining prisoners from Manjaca for exchange, the Special Rapporteur, at paragraph 35, said: "The administrators of Manjaca informed the Special Rapporteur that they look forward to exchanging the prisoners at the earliest possible opportunity. This illustrates the role that the detention of the Muslim and Croat population plays in ethnic cleansing. Those deprived of liberty for no reason except their ethnic origin will be released only on the condition that they leave Serbian-controlled territory." What I'm suggesting to you, Mr. Grujicic, is that's exactly what was happening in Batkovic. These prisoners from Manjaca who had been detained for no reason other than the fact that they were non-Serbs were being taken to Batkovic for their final exchange and plus their ethnic cleansing from Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's why they were in Manjaca, that's why they were in Batkovic, and that's why you're exchanging them, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. If you'd please allow me to explain this. This is a very peculiar case and it has nothing to do with ethnic cleansing. As you said in your question. What is this all about? The commission of the East Bosnian Corps agreed for an exchange with the Tuzla area, and the Tuzla commission comprised Serbs, Croats, and Muslims alike. At that moment, the president of the commission was a Croat. Therefore, Croats and Muslims too went to be exchanged in the Tuzla area. Now, they had agreed upon an exchange, and Tuzla requested specific people who were at Manjaca. The Bijeljina commission asked us if we could send them those prisoners for an exchange, because those prisoners had been requested. We said that this could be done because we too sent requests to the Banja Luka area, requests for specific prisoners. However, when the exchange was about to take place, we sent those people, but the exchange never took place, and only they knew the reasons. In the meantime, we agreed with the same Tuzla Corps for virtually the same group of people to be exchanged, and that's why I spoke to Mr. Velimir Maslic and asked him to speak to Major, representative, for the same people to be returned so that we could exchange them as part of our exchange. If one exchange failed, another would work. That was the line of reasoning behind this. So this was about exchanging prisoners on both sides, and there was no ethnic cleansing involved in the whole thing. So that's what this first passage of what I read is actually about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But having never visited Omarska, Keraterm, Trnopolje, or Manjaca, or seen the records of these judicial proceedings which you say occurred, you've got no idea why these people were detained in Manjaca, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I've said that already, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So you can't disagree with the Special Rapporteur's view that people were detained in Manjaca for the purposes of ethnic cleansing through exchanges, can you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. [Interpretation] Hold on, hold on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think -- Your Honours, this is a classic example of leading the witness to speculate, because the witness had just told us that he knew nothing about this, and now he's asked to speculate what caused the special envoy or the rapporteur to arrive at the conclusion that he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. The Prosecution have -- the witness had said he had never visited these places, and so the Prosecution is putting to him what the Special Rapporteur, who apparently visited these prisoners, had reported. So the question is well placed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You agree that the Special Rapporteur's information on what was occurring in Manjaca is more accurate than yours, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree. I could only speculate about the truth of what this gentleman had written. What I remember is when the all-for-all exchanges were agreed in Geneva between Croats, Serbs, and Muslims, Mr. Schiffer [phoen] was present, or at least that's what I heard, at Manjaca, until the last prisoner left the camp. He was there until the other side fully complied. So I'm unable to speculate who wrote what.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, the Special Rapporteur visited Manjaca; you didn't. All I'm asking you is: Will you accept that the information of someone who actually visited there and inspected facilities would be better than yours, because you didn't? That's all.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but I could have heard this from the other side, had I had the time, but maybe in a different form. So who should I choose to believe? I do not at all accept this, because that has nothing to do with our job or with ethnic cleansing, because we were certainly involved in no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You told me you don't agree with the Special Rapporteur's report. Do you -- what is your -- do you have better information on what occurred and the conditions at Manjaca? If so, can you please tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't have any better information, because, as I said, I was never there. As far as the prisoners I exchanged are concerned, what the rapporteur claims is something I couldn't notice. I may choose to believe, but I may as well refuse to believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Grujicic, as a humanist, you wouldn't have supported paramilitary groups supporting or working with the JNA and Serb authorities in taking over towns by force, detaining prisoners on the basis of their ethnicity, and inhumanely treating them, would you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since 1991, I was a member of the Territorial Defence, and I saw no paramilitary units there. Secondly, the area in which we did our part of the work, in that area there was only the regular army. So as for that, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were aware, weren't you, that "volunteers," in inverted commas, were coming from Serbia and other places to assist the Bosnian Serb military forces in their fight, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I quite understood your question. The line was bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll ask it again. You were aware, weren't you, of "volunteers" - I'm putting that in inverted commas - coming from Serbia and other places to assist the Bosnian Serb military forces in their fight? You were aware of that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could hear these things. But if you say "volunteers," I don't know why you say "volunteers" in inverted commas.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were aware of groups that were called Wolves, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: These were paramilitary groups, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Wolves from Vucjak, in 1991, had the five-pointed star on their caps. It used to be called the Tito cap. They wore JNA uniforms as well. So I have no idea why they should have been considered a paramilitary unit. Later, when they joined the army of the Republika Srpska [as interpreted], they wore the same insignia as the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There was a group called the Wolves of Vucjak, led by Lieutenant Veljko Milankovic, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to Veljko Milankovic, he was not a colonel. He was a lieutenant, and the same that I said before goes for him. They had the insignia of the regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Transcript, because I was listening very carefully to what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On page 34, line 21, here it says: "Later, when they joined the army of the Republika Srpska." The answer that witness gave was: "When the army of Republika Srpska was established." So this doesn't mean they joined, actually, the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you've seen the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's an important point to correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When the VRS, the army of Republika Srpska was formed, are you saying that Lieutenant Veljko Milankovic and his Wolves of Vucjak joined the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was that in 1991 they had the five-pointed star insignia. The moment the JNA left and the army of Republika Srpska was established, they did not join, simply because they were -- they had been born in the area. And the same as all the others who had been born in the area; they automatically became members of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Lieutenant Milankovic, the leader of the Wolves of Vucjak, was a friend of yours, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Mr. Veljko Milankovic was a person I knew. Before that time, we had never met, nor did I ever go to Prnjavor, which is where he hails from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we take our break? We shall take our break and continue at 1100 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, can you hear me again clearly?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Inaudible]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I didn't hear the response. Was that my microphone?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the response.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think now we can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before the break, I was asking you about Lieutenant Veljko Milankovic, the commander of the Wolves of Vucjak, operating in Prnjavor. Are you aware that the Wolves of Vucjak, led by Lieutenant Milankovic, ran a Detention Centre in the Sloga shoe factory in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you regard Lieutenant Milankovic, the commander of the Wolves of Vucjak, as a humanist?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was a fighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you aware that the Wolves of Vucjak, commanded by Lieutenant Milankovic, seized the Kozara transmitter in Prijedor in August 1991, preventing the transmission of television from anywhere other than Banja Luka and Belgrade? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I didn't know anything about that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you know that in April 1992, the Wolves of Vucjak arrested the leader of the SDA, Lisnja, as part of the Serb takeover of that area? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. The leader of the SDS [as interpreted] of Lisnja? Where is Lisnja? Is that a village? Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's SDA, I said, not SDS. Are you aware of that? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you aware that in May 1992 these Wolves of Vucjak, commanded by Lieutenant Milankovic, surrounded -- and other Serbian forces - surrounded the villages of Lisnja and Puraci and demanded that the villagers surrendered their weapons. When they did, they summarily executed four Muslim men? The wolves then set fire to the villages and blew up the mosques. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I wasn't aware of that, nor did I have any opportunity to learn it. I'm not familiar with that area, if you're referring to the municipality of Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you aware that the men from the villages I just -- those two villages were detained at the Sloga shoe factory in inhumane conditions, with overcrowding and inadequate medical care, physical and psychological assault, torture assault and sexual assault? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I was not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were aware that Lieutenant Milankovic was killed, weren't you, during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't killed. He was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And he died in Belgrade? And he died in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he died in hospital. I knew that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you're Captain First Class Milutin Grujicic from Okucani, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And when he died in --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And after he died in hospital, you sent a telegram to Radio Banja Luka in relation to his death --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Just a moment, Mr. Grujicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not object to this line of questioning, but we are now dealing with the area that I touched on yesterday. And as I said yesterday, if a question is to be put to the witness based on a paper - I won't call it a document - this is what I referred to yesterday. I have not had an opportunity to discuss this document with the witness. Your Honours, I don't know if this is a document. I would like you and the Chamber to look at this piece of paper, which is not clear to me, and I do not know how I can put questions on this in re-direct, since I'm not familiar with it. Let me remind you that when Mr. Lukac was testifying before this Tribunal, when I wanted to put questions to him in connection with a radio broadcast, going to his credibility, you made it possible for the Prosecution to get in touch with Mr. Lukac and discuss the document with him. We are now in the same situation, and although the OTP said yesterday they were not going to ask anything about this document, they're evidently going to ask about something that is in this piece of paper, and I have no idea what it's about. That's why I asked yesterday -- yesterday, through my co-counsel, I could have talked about this had the Chamber approved it. I could have discussed this with Mr. Grujicic through my co-counsel. But the OTP said they would not be using it, and now this entire line of questioning concerns this piece of paper. I think this is highly improper. And I would like the Chamber to see this piece of paper and see what it's about, because the OTP has provided me with no information whatsoever about this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The objection is nonsense. I'm asking him whether he sent a telegram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, can you wait?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm simply asking the witness whether he sent a telegram to Radio Banja Luka; that's the extent of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, the Prosecution hasn't said anything about a document. If they're going to -- if they want to introduce that document, they will say so. The last question -- the last question was about whether or not the witness did something which ought to be in his own personal knowledge, and he can answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, when Lieutenant Milankovic, the commander of the Wolves from Vucjak, died, you sent a telegram to Radio Banja Luka, didn't you, in relation to his death?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably did, but I don't see what's bad about this. I think this is normal. I sent similar telegrams to Croatia when Berislav Gagulic was killed, the son of a friend of mine. I also sent a telegram when a colleague of mine, a Muslim, was killed. I sent a telegram to Dzevad Bosnjak. So I don't see what's bad about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You regarded him as a defender of the Serbian people, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, I said that Veljko Milankovic, from Prnjavor, took part in Western Slavonia, where I come from, in the defence of that part of Western Slavonia, and he proved himself, together with the members of all the units, as a fighter who at that moment was separating the warring sides. And when I heard about this misfortune, I certainly sent, through Radio Banja Luka, you say, a telegram of condolence. This is what probably -- what you are probably referring to, a condolence to his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember describing him as a legendary, fearless [Realtime transcript read in error "fatherless"] commander?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm only referring to his participation in Western Slavonia, because that's what I know about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Re. I think for the sake of the transcript, if you look at page 40, line 23. I don't believe I heard you say he was "a legendary, fatherless commander." I thought you said "fearless."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Indeed I did, and I'll ask it again in case there has been any confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. I think it will be corrected. It's clear when they compare with the audio system, it will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A moment ago you said I'm only referring to his participation in Western Slavonia because that's what I know about. It's unclear what you said then. All I'm asking you is: In your telegram, do you remember describing him as a legendary, fearless commander of the Wolves of Vucjak?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember everything, but I can assume, and I do say that's what he was in the area of Western Slavonia. But, as I said, as part of the units of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And do you remember whether you said that Western Slavonia was grieving for you, Lieutenant -- Veljko and the saviour of the Western Slavonia village of Vrbovljani? Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something else now. At the request of the people, a telegram of condolence was sent. I received this telegram on behalf of the people and was asked to pass it on to Radio Banja Luka, because that village is in Posavina, in the area of Okucani, and it was not taken by the Croatian forces, thanks to the units commanded by Veljko, and the people of that area demanded this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. But in this telegram you passed on, did you write on it that you, Captain Milutin Grujicic, Captain First Class of Okucani, held Veljko in the highest regard, swear to him, and that these people of Western Slavonia will never be conquered by strangers? Do you remember putting that on the telegram which went to Radio Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the words you have just spoken are something that I never said, and that is not in the telegram. When you say "strangers," I don't know who you are referring to. Strangers or foreigners. Because we are western -- in Western Slavonia. We were residents of the Republic of Croatia. So there were no foreigners warring against us. It was our former friends, relatives, and acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Did you write --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, haven't you made your point?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Do you have to -- you're taking too long on one matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, yesterday you gave some evidence about an exchange in -- at Christmas 1993. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And I think you said it was so the Croat people could be home for Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said. I repeated the words of Mr. Marko Milos, who said: "Is there any possibility for the Croats to go to midnight mass on their own land?" Because their house was on the other side, where they came from. And that was the agreement between the civilian commissions on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, did you ever go to the village of Zasavica in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you aware that Croats were detained there against their will and isolated from the population of Samac?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of this, because it was only when the corridor was opened up in the direction of Bijeljina that I went to those areas. But I know that at that time there were no camps or prisons on the territory of the municipalities of Samac, Modrica, and the other municipalities in Bosanska Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is your answer to the last question I asked you no, you weren't aware of it? That's all I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no. I wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you regard the homeland -- or the home of people of Croat ethnicity to be Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't me who said that. You didn't understand me just now. I repeated the words of Marko Milos, who was a member of the commission, and that was what he said. I said that those people left their own area, Bosanska Posavina, but the gentleman said this to me on the occasion of the exchange or, rather, the negotiations that took place some ten days before the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, please listen to the question. I was asking you about your views, not someone else's. My next question is in relation to that exchange, in December 1993, the Christmas exchange. Were you aware that some of the people being exchanged that Christmas were in fact coming from Zasavica, in the municipality of Samac, and were being exchanged for people in Croatia? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware. I knew they were from the municipality of Samac. Whether some of them were from the village of Zasavica or somewhere else, I didn't need to know that, because this was a request put in by the Croatian commission for these people to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, if the people were coming from Samac, their home was in Samac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Their home wasn't in Croatia, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But their sons were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: They were being transferred from one country to another, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of their own free will, they applied in the municipal Red Cross in Samac, and on the basis of an agreement between the HVO and the Samac commission, they were taken across, in Dragalic, in the direction of Croatia, and later on towards Orasje.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: They were certainly taken across, but they left their homes, their properties, and all their possessions behind, didn't they, when they went to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. They couldn't take their homes with them. I assume that today, or recently, they have come back. But that's a different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And they left Bosnia-Herzegovina to be swapped for people from Croatia, didn't they, who were going to come and live, Serb people from -- sorry, Serb people from the Croatia control who were going to live in Samac? That's what happened, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But you said --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's incorrect that they were swapped for Serbian people who were going to come and live in Samac? Is that what you're saying? That's not right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't use the word "swapped."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Because these were civilians. Don't say "swapped" or "exchanged." They were civilians. I didn't understand you now. They were not exchanged. If I said that in the municipal Red Cross they applied, they put in applications, and their sons requested this, who were in Orasje, in the HVO formations, so these were requests for the reuniting of families, and the ICRC was present there and they raised no objection to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying it was a one-way transfer, this December 1993 -- not exchange, but just a group of Croats going to Croatia to celebrate Christmas? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
