utterances.text: No, Mr. Re. In fairness to the witness, he has explained the way he understood things. People had applied through the Red Cross, their sons on the other side had asked for them. I think he has explained that. That is his understanding of the situation then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find out if Serbs came from the other side. I'll ask it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, are you saying that that particular -- we can't call it an exchange, according to you, but particular incident, no Serbs came to Bosnia-Herzegovina when the Croats went home for Christmas?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, I'm sure they didn't, because the Croatian side did not respect the agreement that we had reached, which was that they should bring along people we were asking for. But at 1800 hours in the evening. The exchange was carried on only between 1.00 a.m. and 3.00 a.m. They did not respect their part of the agreement, which was why there was no one coming over from the other side. And to make matters worse, when Mr. Marko Milos, on the Croatian side, arrived, he boarded each bus in turn - I don't remember how many buses there were - and --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to stop you there. I just want to clarify. Are you saying there was an agreement between the two sides for an exchange. The Croats didn't respect their side, so the Serbs transferred some people to Croatia, but no one came in return? Is that what you're saying? I just want to get it completely clear.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No, no. Please, I have to ask you again: Don't mention exchange. I'm speaking about the passage of civilians from Croatia to Republika Srpska, and they were supposed to take part of the people who, in the Red Cross, in Slavonia -- Slavonska Pozega or Gradiska, had applied to cross over, they were supposed to bring them along. But they postponed this and they did it later on. But this was only a flow of civilians through certain areas. If you will allow me to tell you --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. All I want to know is: Was it a one-way thing. Did Croat civilians go to Croatia but no Serb civilians came to Bosnia? That's all I want to know, in that particular incident you referred to. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, yes. But a few days later, the Serbs did come from Croatia. That's what they failed to do then, at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, if people had been arrested without charge because of their ethnicity, put into detention centres, tortured, some sexually assaulted, kept in inhumane conditions, beaten daily, and then one day told that they could go for an exchange, and the choice was to go to the exchange or remain behind in the detention centre, subject to daily beatings, inhumane treatment, you'd accept or agree that someone in that situation wouldn't have any choice about going to an exchange, would they?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such a situation, yes, as you're describing it. But again, you are forgetting that I have just said that I'm not aware of any prisons or detention centres in the area of the municipality of Samac, and I said that this was the free will of citizens who applied to the municipal Red Cross. Don't mention beatings or rapes to me. This has nothing to do with it. Many of these people are still expressing their gratitude to me because we helped them do what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You've just said it wouldn't have been voluntary in those situations. The Trial Chamber has heard uncontested evidence from people who were in that situation, uncontested because the lawyers from the accused here haven't challenged that's what happened to them in the detention centres, and these people were taken for exchanges. You would agree, as someone involved in exchanges, that in those circumstances that wouldn't be a voluntary exchange but would be a forcible transfer or deportation, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The witness is led to agree with a statement. We only wish to object the link between the beating and the exchanges. Our line of argument was different all along. So all I'm asking for is for the question to be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. I think you can split.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You agreed a moment ago, Mr. Grujicic, that if people had been in a situation which I described, in inhumane conditions in detention centres, only because of their ethnicity, and given a choice of being exchanged or staying there, possibly being murdered, that that wouldn't be a choice; that would be involuntary? Wouldn't you? You agreed with that. My next question was: If they then went for exchange with someone from the other side, that would be tantamount to a forcible transfer or deportation, wouldn't it, being involuntary?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with you. As I've already explained, the exchanges were carried out exclusively as you said yourself yesterday, for people who had taken part, who had been members in armed units, and it's those people that the exchanges were for, not for the civilian population. What we're talking about now, the so-called Christmas transit, I did say a moment ago that those people had opted to go of their own free will. So I can't answer your question about people being forced, compelled, to go, by hook or by crook. An exchange can only be -- can only take place if both sides agree and it concerns prisoners of war, those who were arrested when carrying weapons and insignia of a certain unit or a certain army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you are winding up?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I've got two areas I wish to cover, Your Honour. One of them is the exchanges. Another one is Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can you do it quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, you just mentioned prisoners of war. The Special Rapporteur, in his report of the 10th of February, 1993, at paragraph 49, said: "The Special Rapporteur believes that only a very small percentage of detainees are genuine prisoners of war. The remainder should never have been imprisoned. Most prisoners are ethnic -- sorry, innocent people who have been seized for exchange, which furthers ethnic cleansing." That's what the Special Rapporteur said about prisoners of war, the people you just mentioned. Do you agree or disagree with his view?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree, because I know nothing about those issues. If that's what has been stated, then it must have been ascertained during talks with the judicial organs. I explained to him the way a prisoner could be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. It was actually ascertained after visiting various detention centres, including Batkovic. Now, you, of course, had the opportunity to see the conditions at Batkovic, didn't you? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the second time that the Prosecution has asked the same question. There was a distinction introduced, the Special Rapporteur visiting the camps, and then he asked Mr. Grujicic to tell us what he knows about it, but he said that he wasn't there, wasn't present. And now for the second time we have the same hypothesis being introduced. Mazowiecki's report dated the 28th of August, 1992, paragraph 35, clearly states that the Special Rapporteur did not visit a single investigation centre. Despite that, the Prosecution is trying to tell us now, for the second time in a row, that the Special Rapporteur did have special knowledge of those. But that's not what it says in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's complete nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, at paragraph 59 of the Special Rapporteur's report of the 10th of February, 1993, he said of Batkovic: "At Batkovic camp, in the north-eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, 1.163 prisoners were kept in what the Special Rapporteur described, after the visit there by his second mission, as two cavernous, unheated storage buildings. Temperatures there dropped between minus 10 and minus 12 degrees Celsius at the beginning of January 1993, and prisoners there face the fight for survival against such temperatures in the winter months still to come." Now, that's what the Special Rapporteur said about conditions at Batkovic before February 1993. I've just read from his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Prosecution has indicated what the Special Rapporteur did. Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were exchanging prisoners from Batkovic. You've already told the Trial Chamber that. You agree with the Special Rapporteur's impression of Batkovic camp following his visit there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree. I've never been to Batkovic. I cannot speak about the conditions there. The only thing I do know is that even in our office, where we worked, we had no heating. I can't confirm something I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, his information, having been there, was better than yours. Are you prepared to concede that he's maybe more accurate than yours and he might be right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I think the point is made. The witness has explained what his position is. Can you move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Grujicic, you told -- I asked you some questions about exchanges and I asked about the one-for-one principle. Could the witness please be shown D162/3 ter, followed by D161/3 ter, which I understand the registry has already. Can you see clearly that document? I know we've had some difficulties. It's a list of 30 people.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we please -- the quality of the image is poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you see that it's a document signed by the commission for the exchange of prisoners, addressed to the Republic of Srpska, Serbian municipality of Samac commission for exchange of the prisoners of war, and arrested civilian in Samac dated the 7th of January, 1993? Can you see that, in this list of 30 people for exchange -- who came to the exchange on the 7th of January, 1993, in Dragalic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can see is a list of names of persons who allegedly came for an exchange on the 7th of January, 1993, in Dragalic. I can only see the list and nothing else. Now I can see the word "Samac" too. Prisoners and civilians who have been arrested. What's that in the upper corner? Serbian municipality of Samac, commission for the exchange of prisoners and arrested civilians, Samac. So we're talking about Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's a document in relation to the people who came to be exchanged in Dragalic, prisoners of war, on the 7th of January, 1993. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you participated in the Dragalic exchanges, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to be there. It was my duty. Because Dragalic straddles the main road in west Slavonia, in the so-called UNPA zone. So only I or another member of the commission were authorised to carry out these exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The answer is yes. I don't want an explanation. You participated. The answer yes. Next document, please. D161/3 ter. Can you see this document clearly? It's a list of prisoners on the same day, but there's a mixture of soldiers and civilians on it.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Again, I see a list, and then above it states, I think -- this is also about Samac municipality. It's not perfectly legible, but I can see that there's a list there bearing the same date -- no, actually, this is the 7th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you read the words "list"? It's in the top and the middle of persons who were exchanged on 7th of January, 1993, in Dragalic -- prisoners? Can you read that? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this list here, it says: Not persons who have arrived but, rather, persons who have left to be exchanged. You said who have arrived. That's not how it reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There's something in the interpretation. Does it say list of persons who were exchanged on 7th of January, 1993, in Dragalic -- prisoners? I'm reading from the English. Can you read that? That's all I'm asking you. List of persons who were exchanged on the 7th of January, 1993, in Dragalic -- prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes, but in order to be a hundred per cent certain, I should check this on the computer. But that's in Banja Luka. I no longer have the data.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Perhaps the Defence counsel could read loud aloud to the witness what it says in the Bosnian, just so we're entirely clear. Could Mr. Lukic assist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. I thought that the document is on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think he's having some difficulty reading it. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ask the witness, then, if he can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, can you read what it says under, I think, "spisak," meaning list?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Persons who left in order to be exchanged on the 7th of January, 1993, in Dragalic -- prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. And you'll see the list contains 30 prisoners -- sorry 30 soldiers and 4 civilians? You can see that, can't you? Yes or no? No explanation, please.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I can see is the list, but I can't tell you who is a civilian and who is a soldier. All I can see is the list itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you see -- can you read the numbers 1 to 30? The last name is Senad Mehmedovic, born 1957.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mehmedovic, Senad, 1950, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you see -- can you see directly below that, there's a heading, civilians, and their full names, Safet Izetbegovic, Andrija Jovic, Marijan Pepic, and Mustafa Pistoljevic, son of Ibrahim, who were said to be civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This was a mixed exchange of civilians and prisoners on the 7th of January, 1993, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This exchange, prisoners were being exchanged for prisoners. But in order to make it easier for the Nepalese battalion to understand and everything concerning the transit, we put everyone there, but we separated civilians from prisoners. And civilians would cross on the basis of a request by the other side. So it was for purely technical reasons that they were put there, but they were separated from the soldiers. So for them, it was not an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown document internal number PDB 83/3 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is it an exhibit or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It will be in a moment. It's a document the Defence have provided to us in disclosure, but the Defence haven't tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's number what?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: PDB -- I've got two numbers. One is 83/3, the other one is 93. I think the more reliable is 83/3. I have copies here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think it was provided yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Re, could you repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: For the record, the number is PDB 83/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, can you see the document on the screen? It's a letter from commission president, Major Jovika Savic, to the Yugoslav government, in relation to an exchange which you went to on the 29th of January, 1993. Can you see the document?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you see that the body of the letter refers to or says: "Pursuant to an agreement between the commission for the exchange of prisoners of the IBK, East Bosnian Corps, 1st Krajina Corps, and the HVO, an exchange of 64 soldiers, 80 civilians, and 50 children, will be carried out on Friday, 29 January 1993, at 1300 hours, in the village of Lipovac, near Sid. We seek your approval and assistance in the conduct of this exchange." You can see that's what it says, can't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can, I can, but not too clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hold on a second, Mr. Grujicic, please. The witness must be shown the entire document. He might be misled if he doesn't see the other half of the document, because all he can see right now is the first half, the first passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure the document can be moved such that he can see the whole contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, I don't want to mislead you in any way. I was just reading to you the body of the first part of the letter. You agree that's what it says, what I just read out to you, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never agreed. I don't know what children this document is talking about. The exchange in Lipovac, there were no children involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please stop. I'm only asking you about the document. Whether I read it out correctly, not your interpretation of it. If I have read it out incorrectly, I'd like you to read out what it says. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this section, the one that you've read out, that seemed accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And on its face, that part of the document indicates that there were negotiations leading to an agreement between your corps, the East Bosnia Corps, the Croatians, for a mixed exchange of soldiers, civilians, and children. That's what it says on its face, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it seems, yes. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I must repeat this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your counsel will clear this up.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The children --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, not at the moment. Mr. Lukic will ask you anything that is necessary. To reach an agreement, you first have to have negotiations in these exchanges, don't you? It's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And there's nothing on the face of this document that indicates there were no negotiations leading to an agreement, is there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, there isn't, for the simple reason that we had completed negotiations and there was supposed to be an exchange taking place in Dragalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't want any more information. Thank you. I'm only asking you about the document. Mr. Lukic wanted you to see the entirety of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can Mr. Usher please move it down so that you can see the remainder of it. I'll give you a chance to read it and then I'll tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you see the balance of the document, if you couldn't see it before?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May the document be tendered into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, as a Prosecution Exhibit. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked P165 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown PDB 84/3. My case manager will -- our case manager will hand to Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, again, my question - I just want you to answer yes - is: Can you clearly see that document and read what it says?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of what I see is that my signature is there. The first name there is Golubovic, then Danijel Pavic, I believe, and I think the third name is Mehmedovic, but I can't be sure. And then Darinka.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you look in the top left hand corner. You'll see it's on the letterhead of your Exchange Commission. The top left-hand corner. Can you see that it says -- and it's referring to the exchange at Lipovac on the 29th of January, 1993, and it says: "List of civilians accepted by us along with soldiers during the exchange that took place in Lipovac village, Sid." Can you see it's saying that there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. And you've said it's your signature. It was a document which -- it's your document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May that be tendered into evidence too, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This next exhibit is P166 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: While that's being done, can the witness please be shown internal number document PDB 86/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you again -- my question is: Can you clearly see the document on the letterhead of your commission, 29th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see now that this is about the dead being exchanged, the dead from Orasje. I see the list too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are 17 names on it. Do you see the 17 names there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you can see the list distinguishes between which are civilians and which are soldiers, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In fact, there are 12 soldiers, 3 civilians, and 2 who are unclassified on that list of 17 people, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And in fact the last one --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Djajic was alive at the time of his exchange.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was he a civilian or a soldier? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. He was a soldier belonging to the Celinac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May that be tendered into evidence too, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just one thing, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: In terms of the numbers, I think, if you look at the B/C/S version, you will see that number 3 on the list, Mr. Danilovic, who does not have a designation after his name, on the B/C/S version there is a ditto mark, indicating that he actually was a soldier as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you, Your Honour, for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I've misled you, Mr. Grujicic. There was actually another soldier on that list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This exhibit is numbered P167 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Grujicic, you've indicated that you regard yourself as a humanist, Mr. Maslic as a humanist, Mr. Tadic as a humanist.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In fact, you had nominated them for awards as humanists, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember now. I may have nominated them, but at this point in time I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You nominated them for a cross of mercy, humanitarian award, and sent a letter to Dr. Simic recommending that they get that award for their valuable humanitarian work, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now I remember. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you regard General Talic as a humanist?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Talic was the Corps Commander and the leader of the entire corps. I consider that we, who only did this part of the job, to be humanists. That means the representatives of the Red Cross, the ICRC. Those are the people I consider to be humanists in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So that excludes Krajisnik, Mladic, Karadzic, and Plavsic as being humanists, does not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, that's not fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Grujicic.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will now talk to you about a few topics on which the Prosecutor examined you. We will clarify some points. I will start from this last document. It doesn't have to be shown to you. It's a document for the exchange of the dead of the 29th of January, 1992, in Lipovac. Do you consider that the exchange of corpses, whether civilian or soldiers, was a humane job?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we had reached an agreement at the level of all the commissions to hand over corpses on both sides. We couldn't put too many questions in wartime as to whether someone who was dead had been exchanged or not. So all we could do was exchange dead bodies. Whether these were soldiers, civilians, children or elderly. The families on the other side asked for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were these handovers of corpses ever done on condition that -- or rather, were any conditions ever imposed on this?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even on that occasion when this was done, I'm not sure, but I think that we did not bring any corpses. It was just an agreement on the part of the commissions that when exchanges of the living take place, we should also exchange corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This last name read out to you under number 17, Grujo Djajic, you said that he was exchanged alive and died on the next day in Bijeljina. What happened? Can you tell us? Don't go into detail, but just tell us: What did he die of?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone was on the bus. Grujo Djajic was carried in in a plastic chair. He was put on the bus. And he was put somewhere in the front part of the bus. In the village of Apcovci [phoen], in the Republic of Serbia, the municipal committee of the Red Cross from Sid organised a dinner for these people. It was a very cold and rainy day. Everyone went out to eat. But we always counted the people, and I noticed one was missing. I sent the driver --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No details, please. I only want to know, in your knowledge, what was the reason for his death? What was the cause of death the next day?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We took him to hospital, and on the next day we learnt that Grujo Djajic had died, that he had been castrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The previous document shown to you by the Prosecutor, P165 - it has now been given a number - I won't ask for it to be put in front of you, but I will read out the second part of that document to you. It is signed by Major General Radovan Radinovic, the president of the commission. In the second part of the document that you have just read, where Major Jovika Savic addresses the Ministry of Defence of the army of Yugoslavia, it says: "We are forwarding to you the information received from the commission for exchanges IBK and the first KK, asking you to make it possible and to assist in this exchange that has already been agreed upon to take place in Lipovac, near Sid, on the territory under UNPROFOR protection." Let me remind you: The first part that you looked at begins with the words: "Pursuant to an agreement, the commission for the exchange of prisoners of IBK and one KK and the HVO," and then the text continues. My question to you is: --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Maybe there's a difference in the translation. The translation I have says: "Pursuant to an agreement between." Between is quite important. The commission, et cetera. If that could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will now read again the entire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Second part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I read the second part of the document, and in view of the fact that the Prosecutor asked the witness whether there had been any negotiations, I'm now putting the first part of the document to the witness. I will read this and then let the witness answer. The first part of the document, Your Honours, if the English translation is not different, I will read only the first two lines: "Pursuant to an agreement between the commission for the exchange of prisoners of the IBK, the first KK, and the HVO, an exchange of 64 soldiers," and so on. This is what it says in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, does it follow from this document that there were negotiations and that an agreement had been reached?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It couldn't be done without negotiations, because, as I explained, there is a procedure for the approval of this. This agreement was reached a long time before between the HVO and these two corps on our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When the civilian commissions wanted to take civilians to be exchanged or, rather, to be allowed to pass through, did they apply to the military commissions to apply for permission on their behalf?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as UNPROFOR is concerned, yes. But as far as I can remember, I never submitted any requests to Yugoslavia, because there was no need for me to do that. It was Major Jovika Savic who did that. He knew the procedure. He knew who he had to ask approval from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that approval was also needed for the passage through Serbia of convoys or buses leaving the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since it occurred unexpectedly that we had to have the exchange in Dragalic, or rather, the exchange had been agreed upon to take place in Dragalic, but as I told the Prosecutor, because of the shooting and the war, we had to do it somewhere else. I called Major Savic, and he said we had to get permission from the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia and the Ministry of the Interior of Yugoslavia, and that this could not be done quickly, and that the exchange might have to be postponed. That's why he asked General Radinovic to help us so that the exchange would go through, and we did get approval from all the relevant organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to the telegram of condolence, you mentioned Berislav Gagulic, that you had sent a telegram of condolence for him. I would like to know the ethnicity of this man.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Berislav Gagulic was a fighter of the Croatian National Guard Corps. He was a Croat from the village of Donji Varos, near Stara Gradiska. His father and I were great friends. And he asked, through mediators, the mayor of Nova Gradiska --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No details, please. I was just interested in his ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Grujicic: When you send a telegram of condolence on your own behalf, do you use the first person singular or the first person plural?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the person in question. In the case of Veljko, the inhabitants of Okucani knew about him, and they knew that I was constantly on the move and that I was in Banja Luka very often. So that on behalf of the entire village, I could be the one to send a telegram of condolence. In the case of the Bosnjak, Dzevad, or Gagulic, I personally felt the need to express my condolences to my friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor today put to you reports by the Special Rapporteur of the UN for the territory of the former Yugoslavia, Mr. Mazowiecki. I will now ask you whether, in the work of your commission, your work on exchanges throughout the period when you worked on these exchanges, did you ever meet Mr. Mazowiecki personally, or any member of his team, in relation to their analysis of human rights violations on the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Nobody visited us. Or rather, nobody from this international body ever attended the exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Part of Mr. Mazowiecki's report was read out to us, saying that people had been robbed before their exchange, that there had been rapes or beatings. Did the opposite side that you negotiated with ever - and we know that you often saw them after an exchange had been completed - did they ever tell you that they had information that women had been raped, that people had been robbed before their exchange? I'm referring to the particular commissions that you worked with, and especially were there any complaints about the Samac commission in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never received any complaints, either from the representatives of the HVO or the Croatian army. Most often they were together, just as we were, from Republika Srpska Krajina and Republika Srpska. We never got any complaints of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive complaints from the opposite side - I'm referring to the military commissions you cooperated with - concerning the treatment of people in the Batkovic collection centre after their exchange?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the exception of the one case that we mentioned here, we had no other complaints. Had there been any, they would certainly have also complained to the international community, which was always present. This, however, did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours who Mr. Milan Duspara is?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marko Duspara.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was first the vice-president of the Tuzla commission, and later on the president of the Tuzla commission for the exchange of prisoners of war, for the entire Tuzla region. His deputy president was Mujcinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Grujicic, we have tendered two video recordings of the exchanges which we did not show you, but Their Honours will analyse them. Tell us: Do you remember that during negotiations in Gradacac, Mr. Duspara, in May 1993, had no complaints against the treatment in Batkovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Several bases. One, is doesn't arise. And secondly, it's cross-examination. In fact, he's given the answer. My learned friend, Mr. Lukic, has given the witness the answer in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I will allow it, Mr. Lukic. You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't mean for the videotape to be shown. I know this question may be slightly leading, and I don't mean to lead the witness. If you remember, please say so; if not, you don't have to say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Duspara, did he have any complaints or objections at any point concerning the treatment of people who had been exchanged and who had come from Batkovic specifically?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Marko Duspara, the Tuzla commission and our commission worked in a responsible and honest way. Had there been any objections or complaints, Duspara would have told me first. I would have blushed. But this never happened. Had this been the case, I would certainly have apologised to the opposite side. But the treatment was correct and our behaviour was mutually correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My colleague from the Prosecution asked you several general questions concerning your views as a humanist. I have two very brief questions, two or three. Please just answer yes or no. Do you know who was in power in Bosanski Samac before the outbreak of war? Do you know about the structure of government in that particular municipality prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, sir, I've never been to Samac, so it follows that I didn't know the ethnic make-up or who was there at different points in time. Only later, when we came, I knew what we had to do and I got in touch with their commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know why people were being arrested or detained in Samac? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge whatsoever of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened in Samac in the night between the 16th and 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. At that time, I was still in Stara Gradiska, because that's where the corps was. So I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only two questions left. The Prosecution showed you sections of a sentencing judgement against Mrs. Biljana Plavsic. My question, specifically, is the following: Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, did she ever attend any of the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I just correct that? It wasn't the sentencing judgement. It was the factual basis for plea of guilty. Just so it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That's correct. I agree, and I apologise. That was a statement regarding the agreement on the guilty plea of Mrs. Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, did she ever attend any of the exchanges that you attended or any of the negotiations related to these exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only was she never there; I never even saw her in Banja Luka. A couple of times on TV perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, did you ever write to Biljana Plavsic or send her any reports on the working method of your commission, describing what the procedure was?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point we received orders specifying that she would cover that particular area. But this only lasted for a very brief while. So it's quite possible that I did indeed send a report or two on the exchanges, because we had received word that she would be in charge of that area. But that soon stopped. Pursuant to what exactly it was, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, if you remember, when and what exactly you wrote.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think I can remember that. It may have been in 1993, but I can't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have finished my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Grujicic, for giving evidence to the Tribunal. We are now finished with your evidence. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we call the next witness after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That was exactly my idea, because we have only several --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we shall start at 12.50 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Will you please state your name.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Savo Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, when were you born, and where?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1943, in the village of Obudovac, Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What's your marital status?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I am married. I have two sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Where do you reside currently?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I reside in Crkvina, Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me: You and your ancestors, how long have you lived in that particular area?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: My ancestors have been here for about 80 or 90 years. My grandfather, my grandfather had arrived in Obudovac as a priest. That's where I was born. I completed elementary school in Obudovac, secondary school in Samac, and then high schooling in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your grandfather and his father originally hail from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from Sekovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: To all intents and purposes, your family roots are in Bosnia and Herzegovina and for several hundred years?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You completed your elementary school in Obudovac?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Secondary school in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: High school for economics in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You are -- you have a degree in economy, in economics; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You did your compulsory military service in the JNA as a communication officer in Osijek in 1969 and 1970?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 1969, 1970, 1971, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your rank in the army, upon completion of military service, was -- you were sergeant first class or senior sergeant?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How long were you a member of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I became a member on the 8th of July, 1963, when I was still in secondary school, and I left the League of Communists in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You probably mean 1988 or 1989.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. 1988, 1989. I had been a member of the League of Communists for 25 or 26 years. I was a leftist by orientation. Even now, in a democratic way. I didn't agree with certain people, but that doesn't mean that I left the whole thing behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You did not disagree with some of the leaders within the League of Communists, but you are still a leftist by conviction?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you currently a member of any party?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am a member of the SDS. In 1993 and 1994 I became a member. So I'm not an active member of the SDS, not as active as I used to be while I was a member of the League of Communists. I am simply a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: However, within that party, you represent the leftist convictions?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am still left-leaning, and I think there is a huge number of people who are leftists. I belong to that group. There are people who became members of that party, because they believed that they could follow their convictions within that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You are referring to your colleagues from the SDS; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As concerns your career, professionally, you were a director of several different companies; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, before the war and during the war, I was serving as a director of a company, so that I have a certain amount of experience, an enormous amount of experience, I should say, and I was in a position to help in many things, in organising the local economy in Samac municipality and also in a more general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When armed fighting broke out in Samac in 1992, you were a director of the Utva factory, the iron construction factory in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was the director of that company, but when I became the director, I put together a mixed company, Jugokovaks together with a German company. It was a joint venture. We started doing serious business, import, export. And towards the end of the 1980s, you could feel that there was tension in the air. I had -- I was facing certain problems related to export. There were a number of scandals because of botched deals. So in 1990 or 1991, I simply left the company, because it was no longer possible, due to its very make-up, to do business. You could feel tension. The atmosphere was charged. I travelled widely. I spoke to my partners from Germany and Holland. I visited the Djuro Djakovic company in Brod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We do have a summary of the subjects for this witness. Can we go to that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour. I will ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Currently you own a private company?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: My son is the owner, actually. I'm there as an advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In addition to your present job, you're also a well-regarded official of the Bosnia and Herzegovina football association?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, for Bosnia and Herzegovina and for Republika Srpska. I hold a number of positions. I'm a member of the Executive Board, chairman of a number of committees. So I am a member of different committees which are part of the football association of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that's where I spent most of my time, with other people who are involved in sports.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, during 1991 and 1992, more specifically, between October 1991 and April 1992, did you witness some political tensions at the republic level, the Bosnia-Herzegovina level, the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Tell us what you know about it, and tell us how those tensions, if any, were reflected on the local level in Samac. Please tell us briefly what you know about the period.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: In that period I was involved in politics, in the period before that I was a member of the municipal committee, I was a member of the League of Communists. I was in the presidency of the Socialists League of Samac municipality, so I was actively involved in politics. But there were disagreements with certain people, as tensions could already be felt. They were mounting in the local politics. Everyone wanted to get it their way. I didn't like that. So I said openly: These are my convictions. Gentlemen, from today, I am no longer a member of the municipal committee. Because what you advocate as Bosniaks, Croats, or Serbs, distinctively, what you're probably driving at is that we should all just best kill each other, and I want no part in that. So goodbye. I was well placed to follow what was going on, those who had gone before me. And when I was there, what the tensions were about. I was following the media, and other sources of information. I knew what people were preparing, what they wanted for Yugoslavia to fall apart, for Slovenia and Croatia to split off. We simply feared that this might spread to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Popovic. My specific question is: Do you have any knowledge of problems faced by the republican parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and if any, were they in any way reflected on the local assembly in Bosanski Samac? Do you have any such information? If not, please say so.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I've been telling you. The sessions were public and they were broadcast, the sessions of the republican parliament. And you could see what people were saying in parliament. It was only to be expected that this would be reflected on the local level. I was surprised that people who had never up to that point discriminated on the national basis suddenly started doing so. This was particularly prominent with Croats, and also my former friends with whom I was spending a lot of time in secondary school, Bosniaks, they started doing the same thing too. And then the gap started widening. Everyone went their own way. Everyone wanted to have things their way. And then the parties emerged, the HDZ, the SDA, and the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How did that look in Samac, specifically? Were they outvoting each other? Were there any tensions between the parties?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, certainly. What followed because of all the outvoting and because of the coalitions that were formed, the policies pursued at that moment, in the former system we had certain decisions that were respected, who the president was going to be or the vice-president of the committee or the party. At one point, Croats and Bosniaks, Muslims, took up all the important positions, and then obviously the third side involved the Serbian side was the underdog in that situation. And we saw what was in store for us. And it is only natural that certain tensions started mounting between people who had been friends up to that point. Now people were becoming mistrustful, or even enemies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You refer to a concept. You said the concept of the key. Was that the national key in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the sense of respecting the respective positions of all the three constituent ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I had in mind. Our own socio-political community respected that. We complied with that. But now it was suddenly no longer what it used to be. Now it was a matter of agreement between certain parties who were now in power. It was a quid pro quo thing. I'll give you a certain position and appoint your people in positions, and you'll give me the same. So it was no longer done the same way as in the former system.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was there any armed conflict or incidents between January 1992 and April 1992 in Samac? Were there any armed units? Did you notice anything along these lines?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: There were provocations in our area constantly since 1991. Just to name one specific example: Croats tried to provoke Serbs. They would have a wedding, celebrate a wedding. And instead of two flags, they would have just one, the Croatian flag, with the chess board. They would drive through the predominantly Serb villages and cause people to revolt. Once in Samac, this was also under the patronage of the SDS [as interpreted], I was coming from my house in Crkvina. There were barricades set up at the entrance to Samac. My workers were there, and they simply wouldn't allow them to enter the city. I smiled and said: Who made you do that? And they simply said: Those who should be manning the barricades, who knows where they were now. And you are here making yourself look laughable. However, what could you do about that? That's what the situation was like. But that was merely an introduction to later events in Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: For the transcript. On page 76, line 21, the witness said "SDA," and here it states "SDS."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, we must be of assistance to both the interpreters and the court reporters. We must be accurate with the concepts that we're using. Can you just pause briefly after I ask my question, because the whole of our communication is being interpreted into our official language, into English, so that we can have an accurate transcript. Did you have any information or did you personally witness the presence of any armed units in Samac, units that were not originally from that area, prior to April 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you: I was in a position to see that, because there was talk that the Zengas and the HVO started appearing in our municipality. In order to check this out for myself, I went and looked, not in Samac, but I crossed the bridge to Prud, and I saw that there were a number of people present there who I didn't know. Some said that they were also moving about Samac. So that in certain areas that were predominantly -- certain people came who were predominantly Croat [as interpreted] and were holding rallies there. This was the case in the municipality of Samac. You could reach it very quickly by bridge or by boat over the river. They could cross easily into our territory of the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Again I have to make a correction of transcript. The witness was referring that he was -- he was talking about predominantly Croat villages and that people who came were predominantly Croats. So it's on page 77, line 23. Maybe if he could speak a bit slower, it would be easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The witness can repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Popovic, you spoke about personally crossing to Prud, which is part of the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please be asked to repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: They said that they were members of the Zenga and the HVO, and it was in that location that I saw a number of people, but I can't say who they were, because I didn't know them. The talk of the town was is that they were all around Samac, in the cafes, in the evening, but I didn't go out in the evenings, so I couldn't see. Their presence was felt in the territory of the Samac municipality, and that in villages and places that were predominantly Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you please tell me about the attitude towards mobilisation and towards the JNA in all of the three different ethnic groups respectively. What do you know about that? Did the JNA send out calls, call-ups, for mobilisation to all citizens, and how did then members of the different ethnic groups relate to mobilisation call-ups?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I think that in our minds we still considered the JNA to be a Yugoslav army, Yugoslavia, that is, Bosnia and Herzegovina still existed, and we had to consider whether to remain or not in the rump Yugoslavia, as it was called. But we all knew that in spite of the mobilisation, the Croats and the Muslims would certainly not respond in the same numbers as before, before it was a hundred per cent, but that they had already prepared where they were to go. We had loyal citizens who remained with us throughout, and they responded to these call-ups, but the others ignored them, and they simply did not wish to respond to these call-ups. I can't give you many details, because I wasn't in the secretariat, so I don't know what the situation was exactly, but this was no longer the army that it used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned the plebiscite of the Serbian people, about remaining in Yugoslavia. I assume that's what you meant. But before we go into that, I would like to ask you whether you know that an assembly of the Serbian people was established in Bosnia and Herzegovina and whether, pursuant to certain decisions, a certain subject was established in Bosnia and Herzegovina in early 1992? What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: As I said at the beginning, I could see from the media what was going on at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and simply --

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: -- Some sort of state, and that's what happened, which is why certain municipalities were created at the level of the entity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: -- The municipalities were given names beginning with Serbian --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're having trouble with the audio over here. We couldn't hear most of the statement. I don't know if the Court could. Could he repeat everything that he said so far?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because there are quite a number of gaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Mr. Popovic, we had some technical difficulties. Would you be so kind as to repeat your answer in connection to your personal knowledge as to whether, within the -- let's call it the national corps of the Bosnian Serbs, an assembly or some other entity was established in early 1992. Could you just repeat what you have said, but briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I was following through the media what was going on, and what charges there were in the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I saw that the parties could not agree that a split was widening among them and that they were setting up their own areas, the Republika Srpska, the Croatian part, the Bosniak part. And this was reflected at the local level, so that certain municipalities began to be created along ethnic lines, the Serbian municipality of Brod, the Serbian municipality of Samac, Bosniak municipality, so-and-so, Croatian municipality, so-and-so, and in this way the Serbian municipality of Samac was established. This happened in the memorial home, and all those who were pro-Serb, including members of all ethnic groups, attended this rally. And what was talked about was how to behave in the situation that had arisen. Yugoslavia was falling apart, and the only thing we could do was -- well, nobody advocated war, but that through this form of organisation, differences could be transcended and we could all remain within Yugoslavia, where the Serbian people wanted to remain, as was seen in the plebiscite. So this was done. The municipality was created, comprising the municipality of Samac and the former municipalities -- or rather, Pelagicevo and Gradacac, whatever they want to call it, the villages from Odzak, so that this municipality consisted of farmers, intellectuals, people of all professions who wanted to attend the rally. Whoever wanted to attend the rally could do so, and this was the beginning of something that would follow later. Therefore, before the outbreak in 1992, a, so to speak, group of people was organised, assemblymen from the broader area in Obudovac, where people were elected, so that in the forthcoming period they could stand up to the wave coming from the SDA and the HDZ, and this was the beginning of the Serbian municipality of Samac, an excellent government was established which could stand up to both sides, and not with a view to war, but simply so that certain solutions could be found in order for us to continue living peacefully, regardless of where someone was, on what territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, I have to ask you again to speak a little more slowly. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please speak more slowly. We have been having some small technical problems. But please tell me now: This first meeting in the cultural -- or in the memorial home, do you remember when it was held?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in late February or early March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At that meeting, was Ilija Ristic elected president of the Serbian Assembly of the municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo, which was being established?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: It was then that this was declared to be the Serbian municipality of Samac --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Stop. Stop, sir. Will you please answer my question. On that occasion, was Mr. Ilija Ristic elected president of that municipality?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ilija Ristic was elected president of that assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Dusan Tanasic elected vice-president of that assembly?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At the next session, please tell me when the next session was held, the session of the Municipal Assembly. Can you tell us the time?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: It was towards the end of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. At that session of the Assembly, did Ilija Ristic remain the president of the Assembly or was somebody else elected? Did he resign? What happened? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: At that session, there was a lot of tension because Mr. Stevan Todorovic wanted, in a way, to be the coordinator of everything that was going on at the Assembly, and pressure was exerted on the way the Assembly was being run. And as far as I know, Mr. Ristic remained the president of the Assembly. As far as I know, at least, there were no changes, but I know that he was -- or rather, that Mr. Mirko Jovanovic became president of the Executive Board. And in the previous government, he had been the president of the Executive Board. I know that other people were nominated to take care of the economy --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, I have to ask you again to slow down. My next question is the following: Did Dr. Blagoje Simic hold any office in that Serbian municipality in the period we are now talking about, that is, from late February, when it was established, until the last -- the second half of April 1992? Have you any knowledge of this? Did he hold any posts?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he could only have been a delegate, as far as I know. And I did follow what was going on at the time, but I'm not aware of him holding any office in the Assembly of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. At this second session of the Assembly in Obudovac, how would you describe the atmosphere? What problems were there? What were the issues being discussed? What was in the air, so to speak, in that period?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I think the main issue was how the Serbian people could organise themselves if the worst happened. That's what they said. If there was a conflict. Because there were intimations that this was possible, since both sides were arming themselves. The problem was how to make sure that the government functioned, the economy functioned, health care and the infrastructure in general continued to function. At that session of the Assembly, there were a number of delegates from the area of the municipality of Odzak who were deeply concerned because of events in Odzak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, again there's a technical problem. Mr. Popovic, when you mentioned the problems of all three sides, you said that both sides were arming. What both sides did you mean? Could you be more precise and tell us what ethnic group those sides belonged to?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'll be specific. The Croatian side, through the HDZ; and the Bosniak people, through the SDA. I assert with full responsibility that the Serbs did not do this, because they felt that the army of Yugoslavia was present in Bosnia and Herzegovina and they felt no need to obtain weapons. You asked me about the mobilisation and who responded and who didn't. Well, for the most part, it was the Serbs who responded, and they were already in those units, so there was no reason for them to arm the general population, at least until that moment, that never entered the minds of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, according to your personal knowledge, whether the SDS had armed formations in Samac.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was not a single armed formation belonging to the party. What there was, was due to the regular mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Popovic. My colleague is asking me to check the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Mr. Popovic. There's something we have to clarify. It's not very precise on the record. My question is: According to your personal knowledge, can you tell us whether the SDS in Samac had armed formations? Just say yes or no so that the answer is very precise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat the answer? The interpreters didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At the same time, did you have personal knowledge as to whether members of other parties besides -- or rather, parties except for the SDS had armed formations? If you know, tell us.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that the SDA and the HDZ were arming themselves, and this could be seen because there were checkpoints and so on and they were transporting weapons. In the case of Samac, it was from Gradacac and other places. They were making use of all sorts of things. Let me give you an illustration. They would take hunting dogs and put weapons in their cars and drive to Samac in this way, and then distribute weapons to certain people. They knew exactly to whom they should give weapons and to whom not. They knew who was loyal and who was not. Those who were not loyal, they could get weapons. So that is the response to the mobilisation. Those who were Bosniaks or Croats and who responded to the mobilisation, they were not given weapons because they did not trust them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. I just want the witness to indicate whether this is personal knowledge or is this some rumours that he heard. Did he actually see this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The question started with: Did you have personal knowledge ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If that's his indication he had personal knowledge, that's fine. It just wasn't clear from the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, before the break, just one further question --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I thought we have a break, but we are working 15 minutes more. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Popovic, in the period before the outbreak of armed conflict in Samac, in Crkvina, did you hold any political office or socio-political office? If so, tell us what it was.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Being a long-time resident of Crkvina, I discharged a number of duties. I was the president of the local commune, the secretary of the local party branch, the president of the local organisation of the socialist league. I was the president of the local football club. So it was all about a number of people who were there who were active and held positions. We were part of the infrastructure of the local commune. So yes, I did hold a number of offices, and I was active in the political life and cultural life and sports life of the local commune and in a broader area at that time. So yes, I was actively involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you hold any specific office at the local commune in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I was not the president. I was a member of the board of the local commune at that moment. I was a member of the board.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the period prior to mid-April 1992 and then all the way to the end of 1993, did you ever attend any political rallies organised by the SDS, where ethnic intolerance or even hatred was advocated?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, there wasn't a single rally like that, even in our local commune, people did get together, but there was never any discrimination, and no hatred was being whipped up. It was a simple matter of how to organise ourselves and how to preserve our property and our families. That was the main motive behind the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In view of the rising tensions in Samac and in the surrounding area, did you have any personal knowledge, direct knowledge, rather, or you may have heard from someone else, that an attack was being prepared on Samac in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: What I said to you, this was organised ahead of time. Weapons were collected and given to certain people --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness so far has testified to no involvement in the 4th Detachment or any detachments within the municipality of Samac. He hasn't testified to any involvement with the JNA, any involvement with military intelligence, any involvement in any sort of military or armed force. If he is going to indicate that he has knowledge, he should state what the facts are and exactly what the basis of that knowledge is. Other than that, it's speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was of the impression that the witness will explain what is the sources of potential knowledge or basis for this possible knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because your question did include: Did you have any personal knowledge, direct knowledge, and things like that. So it's really the way the witness is answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And then, in addition to that, in his summary, he indicates personal knowledge of possible Muslim/Croatian -- or is it possible Muslim/Croat attack. So are we just talking about speculation here and his personal views and maybe because people are arming they were going to attack, or does he have concrete knowledge? And if he doesn't have concrete knowledge, then this is all inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps Mr. Pantelic can ask the witness to explain whether he actually witnessed anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That was exactly my line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Popovic, can you tell us the following: Did you have any personal knowledge or information about a possible attack by the Croat or Muslim forces on Samac in April 1992? If so, please explain what your sources were, how you obtained that information. If not, simply tell us that you didn't. Just slowly, please. It's difficult for the interpreters to keep up with you.

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you the following: I learned this from the secretary of the secretariat for National Defence, Mr. Milos Bogdanovic. He told me. He was practically in charge of the mobilisation. And in the information, there was also word of what was happening, what was being done in Samac municipality and a broader area. We were on visiting terms, and he didn't tell me on which specific day it would happen, but on the basis of all the information that he had, all the available information, he said that the SDA and the HDZ were preparing to take the town of Samac. That's my answer to your question. That's how I obtained my information. He told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Then this witness --

utterances.speaker: SAVO POPOVIC
utterances.text: -- And that's an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This is multi-level hearsay. This witness has no personal knowledge. He should be at least -- counsel should explain to him when he asks him what personal knowledge is, what exactly he's asking for. This isn't personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But we can move on. The witness has explained. Mr. Pantelic, you can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
